etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English renderen, rendren, from Old French rendre (“render, give back”), from Late Latin rendere, from Latin reddere (“make, give back”).

definitions.definition: (ditransitive) To cause to become.

quote.citation: 1918, W[illiam] B[abington] Maxwell, chapter VII, in The Mirror and the Lamp, Indianapolis, Ind.: The Bobbs-Merrill Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: […]  St. Bede's at this period of its history was perhaps the poorest and most miserable parish in the East End of London. Close-packed, crushed by the buttressed height of the railway viaduct, rendered airless by huge walls of factories, it at once banished lively interest from a stranger's mind and left only a dull oppression of the spirit.

quote.citation: 2022 November 2, Paul Bigland, “New trains, old trains, and splendid scenery”, in RAIL, number 969, page 57:
quote.text: This service has suffered badly from Department for Transport-inspired cuts which reduced it from hourly to two-hourly. This, coupled with regular cancellations, has rendered the train service between the area's two biggest towns almost unusable.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To interpret, give an interpretation or rendition of.

quote.citation: 1748, David Hume, Enquiries concerning the human understanding and concerning the principles of moral., London: Oxford University Press, published 1973, § 34:
quote.text: we may, at last, render our philosophy like that of Epictetus

definitions.definition: (transitive) To translate into another language.
(transitive) To pass down.
(transitive) To make over as a return.
(transitive) To give; to give back; to deliver.

quote.citation: 1725, Isaac Watts, Logick: Or, The Right Use of Reason in the Enquiry after Truth, […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  John Clark and Richard Hett, […], Emanuel Matthews, […], and Richard Ford, […], published 1726, →OCLC:
quote.text: Logic renders its daily service to wisdom and virtue.

quote.citation: 1980, AA book of British Villages, Drive Publications Ltd, page 164:
quote.text: The first thing that greets you on entering the church is a notice asking you not to vex the goat, since it renders valuable service in keeping the churchyard tidy.

definitions.definition: (transitive, dated) To give up; to yield; to surrender.

quote.citation: c. 1595–1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “A Midsommer Nights Dreame”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: I'll make her render up her page to me.

definitions.definition: (transitive, computer graphics) To transform (a model) into a display on the screen or other media.
(transitive, art, by extension) To apply realistic coloring and shading.
(transitive) To capture and turn over to another country secretly and extrajudicially.
(transitive) To convert waste animal tissue into a usable byproduct.
(intransitive, cooking) To have fat drip off meat from cooking.
(construction) To cover a wall with a layer of plaster.
(nautical) To pass; to run; said of the passage of a rope through a block, eyelet, etc.
(nautical) To yield or give way.

quote.text: The rope of a laniard or tackle is said to render when, by pulling upon one part, each other part takes its share of the strain.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To return; to pay back; to restore.

quote.citation: 1596, Edmund Spenser, “Book IV, Canto X”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 14:
quote.text: whose smallest minute lost, no riches render may

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To inflict, as a retribution; to requite.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Deuteronomy 32:41:
quote.text: I will render vengeance to mine enemies.

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable) Stucco or plaster applied to walls (mostly to outside masonry walls).
(computer graphics) A digital image produced by rendering a model.
(obsolete) A surrender.
(obsolete) A return; a payment of rent.

quote.citation: 1765–1769, William Blackstone, Commentaries on the Laws of England, (please specify |book=I to IV), Oxford, Oxfordshire:  […]  Clarendon Press, →OCLC:
quote.text: In those early times the king's household was supported by specific renders of corn and other victuals from the tenants of the demesnes.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) An account given; a statement.

quote.citation: c. 1605–1608, William Shakespeare, “The Life of Tymon of Athens”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: And send forth us , to make their sorrow'd render, Together with a recompense more fruitful Than their offence can weigh down by the dram

etymologies.etymologyHTML: rend +‎ -er

definitions.definition: One who rends.

quote.text: Oh, this render of hearts, this murderer of love, this perpetual crucifier of Christ,  […]
